metadata.title: Creative thinking, mathematics achievement, and well-being: A multilevel analysis of Spanish students
metadata.venue: International Journal of Educational Research Open

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the OECD PISA 2022 nationally representative sample for Spain, with students nested within schools (two-level structure). The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme, and it instead focuses on multilevel linear models estimated in R (lme4). Because the analysis is multilevel and uses PISA-derived scaled scores/WLEs/PVs, analysts should consult the OECD PISA Public Database documentation for the appropriate student weight variable(s) and replicate weights if variance estimation under the complex design is required. In the absence of explicit weight application in the paper, results should be interpreted as model-based associations rather than fully design-weighted population estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the nationally representative PISA 2022 student sample for Spain. Cases with missing data on any core demographic variables were deleted using listwise deletion, yielding the final analytic sample of 30,800 students nested in 966 schools. For the School Creative Environment variable, which had ~97.19% missingness due to PISA rotational questionnaire design, the authors performed multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) and then conducted primary analyses using the first imputed dataset to avoid interpretive complexity.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel linear models (two-level HLM). Model 1: Creative Thinking β=3.95 (p<.001). Model 2: School Avg. Creative Thinking β=2.54 (p<.001). Model 3 interaction (Creative Thinking × SES): β=0.01 (p=.691). N=30,800; Schools=966; R2 fixed: 0.34 (M1), 0.39 (M2), 0.34 (M3); R2 total: 0.39, 0.42, 0.39.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 (Spain) Mathematics literacy data with PV1MATH, the study leveraged Creative thinking performance, Creative self-efficacy, socioeconomic status (ESCS), gender, and immigration background to predict mathematics achievement, finding that creative thinking was a strong positive predictor (β=3.95, p<.001) and that school-average creative thinking also remained significant (β=2.54, p<.001). The Creative Thinking × SES interaction was not significant (β=0.01, p=.691), indicating the relationship was similar across socioeconomic groups. This indicates that integrating creative-thinking development into both classroom instruction and school-level learning culture may support mathematics achievement without widening socioeconomic disparities, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel linear models (two-level HLM). Model 1: Creative Self-Efficacy β=0.16 (p<.001); Creative Thinking β=-0.03 (p<.001). Model 2: Creative Thinking × School Creative Env. β=-0.02 (p<.01) (interaction reported as not significant in text); School Creative Env. β=0.13 (p<.001); School Avg. SES β=0.06 (p<.001). N=30,800; Schools=966; R2 fixed: 0.07 (M1), 0.07 (M2), 0.07 (M3); R2 total: 0.08 across models.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 (Spain) Life satisfaction data with WLE (LIFE-SAT), the study leveraged creative thinking performance, creative self-efficacy, socioeconomic status (ESCS), gender, and immigration background to predict life satisfaction, finding that creative self-efficacy was a significant positive predictor (β=0.16, p<.001) while creative thinking had a small but significant negative association (β=-0.03, p<.001). The moderation test with school creative environment did not show a meaningful difference in the creative thinking–well-being link (interaction not supported in the main text). This indicates that policies and school practices should prioritize building students’ creative self-beliefs (confidence and persistence) to improve well-being, rather than assuming that higher measured creative performance alone will raise life satisfaction.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel linear model (two-level HLM). Model 1: Creative Self-Efficacy β=0.10 (p<.001); Creative Thinking β=0.01 (p=.218, not significant). Student SES β=0.04 (p<.001); Gender (Female) β=0.67 (p<.001); Immigrant Background β=0.06 (p<.001). N=30,800; Schools=966; R2 fixed=0.14; R2 total=0.14; AIC=78306.56; BIC=78373.24.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 (Spain) Stress resistance data with WLE (STRESAGR), the study leveraged creative thinking performance, creative self-efficacy, socioeconomic status (ESCS), gender, and immigration background to predict stress resistance, finding that creative self-efficacy was a significant positive predictor (β=0.10, p<.001) while creative thinking performance was not significant (β=0.01, p=.218). This indicates that strengthening students’ creative self-efficacy may be more effective for improving stress resilience than focusing solely on measured creative performance, though the cross-sectional PISA design prevents causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses OECD PISA 2022 microdata for Spain (15-year-olds; 30,800 students in 966 schools) to examine how creativity-related factors relate to mathematics achievement and well-being using two-level multilevel linear models. Mathematics achievement is modeled with PV1MATH (first plausible value), while life satisfaction (LIFE-SAT) and stress resistance (STRESAGR) are modeled using WLE questionnaire scales. The key results show that creative thinking performance strongly predicts mathematics achievement (β=3.95, p<.001) and that school-average creative thinking remains significant after student controls (β=2.54, p<.001), whereas the Creative Thinking × SES interaction is not significant (β=0.01, p=.691). For well-being, creative self-efficacy is the consistent positive predictor (life satisfaction β=0.16, p<.001; stress resistance β=0.10, p<.001), while creative thinking has a small negative association with life satisfaction (β=-0.03, p<.001) and is not significant for stress resistance. Limitations include cross-sectional associations and primary analyses using only the first plausible value, plus the paper’s explicit use of MICE for a rotationally missing school variable but no reported design-weight application.
